content.thinking:
I should avoid restating the given figures as if I'd computed them myself, and not offer my own number either—the actual cost was derived from what the shop took in, and the impact duration is just a lower bound with an unknown error rate, so I need to be careful not to quantify things on my own.

The root cause was a derived cache of spend totals falling out of sync with the authoritative purchase ledger, while the ledger itself stayed correct and the service remained healthy; the trigger is unknown since no deploys, flags, logs, or metrics are retrievable. I'm treating onset as the alert time since no prior metrics exist, assuming the ledger was authoritative, that discarding stale entries resolved things even without post-fix confirmation, and that duration can only be stated as a lower bound since recovery was never observed in metrics—importantly, the 0.02 hours tracked by Argus was response time, not fault duration, so I shouldn't conflate the two. Now I'm writing up the executive summary, avoiding component names where possible and just describing that a saved copy of customers' spending totals stopped matching the authoritative records.

assumptions: The onset is assumed to be the alert time (21:27 UTC). Zero minutes of metrics were returned, so the fault may have begun earlier and gone undetected.

The duration is a lower bound, not a measurement: no recovery was observed in any metrics window, and the time Argus held the incident (roughly a minute) measures the response, not how long the service was wrong.
Error rate and user-facing impact are unknown — the metrics for the incident could not be read, so no impact figure is offered.

The purchase ledger is assumed to be the authoritative and correct source, and the cached totals the only thing diverging; this follows the investigator's reading rather than an independent verification.

The absence of deploys, flag changes, config changes and log lines is absence of retrievable records, not evidence that no change occurred. The triggering change, if any, is outside the queried windows.
The mitigation is assumed effective because the store reported which stale entries it discarded; there were no post-fix metrics confirming the cached totals returned to agreement with the ledger.
It is assumed the divergence would not immediately recur after the discarded entries were rebuilt, since the underlying sync defect was not identified.
input.executive_summary: A saved copy of customer spending totals in the shop service drifted out of step with the underlying record of purchases. The purchase records themselves were always correct and nothing was down, slow or erroring — the only fault was that some of the pre-computed totals served from the saved copy were out of date, so anyone reading those totals could have seen figures that did not match the purchases behind them. The problem was detected automatically at 21:27 UTC on 6 October 2026. The investigation could not retrieve any metrics, logs or change records for the service, so the start of the fault is assumed to be the moment the alert fired, and no recovery was observed in the data available: the length of the disruption can only be stated as at least the interval from detection to the fix, which is a floor rather than a measurement. How many customers or requests saw wrong totals is not known and is not quantified here. Responders cleared the affected out-of-date totals so they would be rebuilt from the purchase records, and the store confirmed what it had removed; this was judged to address the whole of the fault. A draft code change has been proposed for follow-up.
input.root_cause: A derived, optional cache of spend totals for io-shop (io-summary-cache) stopped being kept in sync with the purchase ledger behind it, so a subset of cached totals disagreed with the authoritative purchase history while the ledger itself remained correct and the service stayed healthy and responsive. What caused the cache to stop tracking the ledger was not established: no deploy, release, flag or config change was recorded anywhere in the lookback, no log lines were returned for any window queried around the onset or the alert, and no per-minute metrics could be read, so any triggering change lies outside what was retrievable during the investigation.
